title: What is Shadow AI? Definition, Risks & How to Detect It (2026 Guide)
summary: Shadow AI is any AI tool or agent used at work without approval. The definition, seven risks, the shadow AI agents nobody registered, and how to govern them.
body_markdown:
**Shadow AI** is any AI tool, model, agent or AI-powered feature that employees use for work without approval, review or oversight from IT, security, legal or data governance. A personal ChatGPT account, a browser extension that summarizes tickets, an AI notetaker silently joining calls, a coding assistant reading the repo, a Zapier automation posting to Slack on a shared login. It is shadow IT with a much shorter fuse, because the thing being handed over is not a login. It is your data.


What shadow AI looks like once you can see it: every unsanctioned AI tool and agent, how Strac found it, who uses it, which sensitive data it can reach, and a one-click decision to sanction it with an owner or block it.


In 2026 the definition has to stretch one more step. The shadow AI tool of 2023 was a chat tab. The shadow AI of 2026 is increasingly an agent: software that holds a standing OAuth grant, an API key or a human's browser session, decides its own next action, and keeps running when nobody is watching. That is why this guide treats shadow AI agents as a first-class category, and why Strac's answer has grown from discovery plus redaction into a full[AI agent security](https://www.strac.io/blog/ai-agent-security) platform.


This guide covers the definition, why the problem is compounding, real examples, the seven risk categories, how detection methods compare, the MCP and agent wave, a policy that holds, and how Strac discovers, governs and controls shadow AI and shadow AI agents.


## Shadow AI, in Short


Finding shadow AI is step one. Ranking what to do about it is step two, which is what[AI security posture management](https://www.strac.io/ai-security-posture-management) adds: each tool and agent gets a risk finding in plain words instead of a flat list.


The three questions people actually need answered:


- **Why it matters:** the data does not come back. A patient record pasted into a consumer chatbot may be retained, used to improve a model, and in some tiers reviewed by a human. There is no recall.
- **How to detect it:** browser telemetry, egress and DNS logs, OAuth grants in your identity provider, endpoint visibility and expense reports. Each catches a different slice, and none catches all of it. See the detection table below.
- **What to actually do:** banning it fails, because the tools are useful and one tab away. What works is letting people use AI while sensitive data is stripped out of the prompt before it is submitted, and giving every agent an owner, a scoped credential and an audit trail.


That last point is the whole game. **Shadow AI is not a discovery problem you solve once; it is an enforcement problem you solve continuously.** A list of unsanctioned tools is obsolete the week a new one launches. A control that redacts PII, PHI, card data and secrets out of any prompt, in any AI tool, on any account, does not go stale. Neither does a graph that shows which agent can reach which sensitive data.


## What is Shadow AI?


**Shadow AI is the use of any AI tool, model, agent, or AI-powered feature inside an organization without explicit approval, review, or oversight from IT, security, legal, or data governance.**


It includes the obvious cases:


- ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity used through personal accounts in the browser
- GitHub Copilot, Cursor and Replit AI installed on developer laptops without licenses tracked
- Midjourney, DALL-E and Runway used by marketing without procurement
- AI Chrome extensions added by individual employees


And the less obvious, and often more dangerous, cases:


- AI features auto-enabled inside already-approved SaaS: Notion AI, Slack AI, Atlassian Intelligence, Salesforce Einstein, Zoom AI Companion
- AI Chrome extensions and agentic browsers (Comet, Dia) that read every page the user visits
- OAuth grants where a single employee gave an AI app full read access to corporate Google Drive, Gmail or Slack
- Custom GPTs, Copilot Studio agents, Agentforce bots and Glean assistants built by individual teams, often with no named owner
- Locally run MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers connecting LLMs to filesystems, databases and SaaS APIs
- Computer-use agents and automations (Cowork, Zapier, n8n) acting inside a human's logged-in session or on a shared account


The term is a direct extension of **Shadow IT** , the 2010s-era category for unsanctioned SaaS apps, applied to the AI wave that started with ChatGPT in late 2022. Shadow AI inherits every problem Shadow IT had and adds three new ones: prompt-level data leakage, prompt injection, and the fact that the model itself is a third-party data processor whose retention and training behavior is often unclear.


### Shadow AI meaning vs. Shadow AI definition


The two phrases get used interchangeably. The cleanest working definition for security and compliance teams:


> Shadow AI is any AI capability used by employees, contractors, or systems inside the company that has not been inventoried, risk-assessed, or governed under the organization's AI policy.


If you cannot answer "who used what AI tool, with what data, when, and under whose authorization," it is shadow AI. If you cannot answer "what is this agent, who owns it, what identity does it run as, what can it reach, and what did it do," it is a shadow AI agent.


## Why Shadow AI is exploding in 2026


Shadow AI grew faster than any prior Shadow IT wave. Four structural reasons:


**1. Adoption is bottom-up.** Employees adopt AI tools faster than security can review them. A tool goes from "I saw it on Twitter" to "embedded in our daily workflow" in under a week.


**2. Free tiers eliminate the procurement gate.** Every consumer-grade AI has a free or low-cost individual tier with no SSO, no admin console, and no audit logs from the customer's side.


**3. The browser is the new perimeter, and most security teams don't own it.** AI tools are accessed through` chat.openai.com` ,` claude.ai` ,` gemini.google.com` . Network firewalls see TLS-encrypted HTTPS to a known SaaS domain. They do not see the prompts, the file uploads or the OAuth scopes granted.


**4. AI is being shipped *into* every SaaS the company already pays for.** Microsoft, Google, Slack, Notion, Atlassian, Salesforce, Zoom, GitHub: every major SaaS now has AI features that are "free" with the existing license. You don't have to install anything to be using AI. Often you have to opt *out* , and the opt-out is buried in admin settings.


The result: by Q1 2026, large enterprises that have done full shadow AI discovery audits are typically finding **8–12× more AI tools in active use than their security team had on file** . Mid-market is similar in proportion, just smaller in absolute terms.


## From shadow AI tool to shadow AI agent


The same employee, three months apart, moves through three stages. Each stage changes what is exposed and which control works.


Stage


What it looks like


What is exposed


The control that works


1. Shadow AI tool


A ChatGPT tab on a personal account


Whatever gets pasted, once, by a human


Redact at the prompt; discover the tool in the browser


2. Shadow AI connector


The same user builds a GPT or Claude project and clicks "Allow" on a Google Drive connector


Standing read access to every file the user can open, with no human reviewing each read


Inventory OAuth grants, resolve scopes to sensitive files, revoke or narrow


3. Shadow AI agent


Claude Code with` contents:write` on a repo, an MCP server with shell access, a Zapier flow on a shared CRM login, an Agentforce bot nobody owns


Standing read, write, send and execute, exercised without a human in the loop


Identity, permissions, activity and data in one graph; owner required; least privilege measured over a window


Stage 1 is a data-handling problem. Stage 3 is an identity and permissions problem that happens to involve AI. Most shadow AI programs were built for stage 1. The rest of this guide covers all three.


## ✨ Shadow AI examples: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and the tools employees really use


The most common shadow AI tools are the famous ones: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and Perplexity, used on personal accounts in the browser or through desktop apps. The riskier long tail is notetakers, coding assistants, AI extensions and agents. Every example below is a real pattern observed in customer shadow AI discovery scans (anonymized):


- A backend engineer pastes a production database connection string into ChatGPT to debug a slow query. The conversation is now in OpenAI's training-eligible logs.
- A sales rep uploads a CSV of 14,000 customer contacts into Claude to draft personalized follow-ups. Customer PII leaves the company perimeter.
- A finance analyst summarizes pre-release quarterly numbers in ChatGPT. Material non-public information is now in a third-party log.
- A marketing manager uses Jasper to draft a launch announcement two weeks early. The unreleased product name and pricing sit in a vendor's database.
- An employee installs an "AI meeting notetaker" extension that records every Zoom and Google Meet call, including the executive offsite where M&A is discussed.
- Notion AI is left enabled organization-wide. It indexes the entire workspace, including private HR pages, and serves answers to anyone with a Notion account.
- A developer authorizes GitHub Copilot in their personal account to access all corporate repos, including the one with hard-coded AWS keys.
- A new "agentic browser" is installed by 30 engineers. Every page they visit, including corporate admin consoles, is streamed to the browser vendor's LLM.
- An MCP server on a developer laptop is given filesystem and shell access. It reads` ~/.ssh/id_rsa` ,` .env` files and browser cookie databases as context for routine prompts.
- A RevOps lead wires a Zapier "lead sync" automation into Salesforce on a shared team login. Salesforce's audit log attributes every record update to the team account, not the automation.


When a shadow AI discovery scan is run against a typical mid-market company, the inventory looks something like this:


The famous tools sit at the top, but the 37% going to unmanaged AI is where regulated data leaves unseen. A visit is recorded as a hostname, never the prompt.


## ✨ Shadow AI risks: the 7 categories that matter


Shadow AI is not one risk. It is seven distinct risk categories, and a complete program needs to address all of them.


Two of the seven are about data leaving, three about compliance and audit, and two about access that an AI tool or attacker can abuse. One control set covers all of them: redact at the prompt, inventory grants, and give every agent an owner.


**1. Sensitive data exposure.** PII, PHI, PCI, source code, customer lists, credentials and trade secrets pasted into prompts. Free-tier consumer AI tools generally retain prompts and may use them for model improvement. Even paid enterprise tiers retain prompts for 30 days for abuse detection. The 2023 Samsung incident, where engineers leaked semiconductor design code into ChatGPT, is the canonical example, but variations happen weekly inside most companies.


**2. Compliance and regulatory violations.** Shadow AI breaks every major framework:


- **SOC 2** : CC1.4 (vendor risk), CC6.1 (logical access) and CC9.2 (third-party risk) all assume an inventory of services processing customer data. Unauthorized AI tools are unmanaged third-party processors.
- **GDPR** : Article 28 requires a data processing agreement with every processor. A consumer ChatGPT account does not have one.
- **HIPAA** : sending PHI to an AI vendor without a Business Associate Agreement is a per-record violation.
- **PCI DSS 4.0** : Requirement 4 covers transmission of cardholder data; pasting card data into a prompt is an undocumented external transmission.
- **EU AI Act** : Article 26 places obligations on deployers of AI systems. "We didn't know our employees were using it" is not a defense.
- **ISO 42001 and NIST AI RMF** : both require an inventory of AI systems and a risk management lifecycle. Shadow AI is, by definition, outside the inventory.


**3. Intellectual property leakage.** Anything submitted to a free-tier AI may be retained, indexed or used to train future models. For pre-release products, undisclosed financials or proprietary code, this is a one-way leak.


**4. Data residency and sovereignty violations.** Most consumer AI tools route prompts through US-based infrastructure regardless of the user's location. EU and APAC employees pasting EU resident data into ChatGPT may trigger cross-border transfer obligations under GDPR, the UK Data Protection Act and emerging APAC privacy laws.


**5. OAuth and over-permissioned grants.** Often the most under-appreciated risk. An employee installs an AI app from the Google Workspace Marketplace and clicks "Allow." That single click can grant the vendor read access to every email, Drive document and calendar entry, and the grant persists until manually revoked, even after the employee leaves. In Strac's agent inventory this is the most common way a shadow AI tool becomes a shadow AI agent.


**6. Prompt injection and indirect attack surface.** AI tools that read external content (web pages, emails, Slack messages, support tickets) are exposed to adversarial instructions hidden in that content. Every shadow AI tool with broad data access is a new injection target, and an agent with write or execute capability is a target that can act.


**7. Audit trail gaps.** When the IT team does not know a tool is in use, there are no logs. When something goes wrong (a leaked prompt, a customer complaint, a regulator's question) the company cannot reconstruct what happened. The absence of logs alone is a finding under SOC 2, ISO 27001 and HITRUST.


A modern shadow AI program needs to surface, in one view, which AI tools are creating risk in which category, at the tool level and at the user level:


Each line carries the user or agent, the evidence source and the data class involved, so remediation starts with a conversation with one person rather than a company-wide memo.


Risk scoring should weight not just *what* AI tool is in use but *what data* has flowed into it, *who* the user is, and *what permissions* the tool has been granted in the rest of the SaaS estate.


## Shadow AI vs. Shadow IT vs. AI Governance


These three terms collide constantly. The differences:

Shadow AI is the *discovery and remediation* layer. AI governance is the *policy and lifecycle* layer above it. You cannot govern what you have not discovered, which is why shadow AI detection is the prerequisite for any serious[AI agent governance](https://www.strac.io/blog/ai-agent-governance) program. The row that should worry you is **Reversible** : shadow IT is a governance problem you can unwind, shadow AI is a disclosure you cannot take back.


## ✨ Shadow AI detection: can CASB, EDR or DLP find it? The 5 methods that work


The short answer to "can CASB detect shadow AI?" and "can EDR detect shadow AI?" is: partly. A CASB or secure web gateway sees traffic to AI domains it already knows and the sanctioned apps it brokers, but not a personal account on a home network, a tool that launched last week, or an agent acting through an OAuth grant. EDR sees AI desktop apps and processes running on a device, but it is built to catch malware, so it does not classify what data went into a prompt and it does not see the prompt in a browser tab. Traditional DLP watches email, uploads and egress. Shadow AI detection that holds up needs content-aware visibility in the browser and on the endpoint, joined with OAuth and audit-log evidence.


CASB, EDR and OAuth scans each see one slice of shadow AI. Only browser and endpoint DLP see the data itself, which is why Strac uses them as the base layer and adds provider evidence on top.


Most security teams start with network logs and find very little, because AI usage is browser-based, SaaS-embedded and OAuth-driven. Real shadow AI detection fuses five sources, ranked from highest signal to lowest:


**1. Browser-level and endpoint discovery.** A lightweight browser extension or an already-installed endpoint agent that observes domain visits, prompts typed, files uploaded, clipboard pastes and local agent processes. This is the only signal that captures *what data* is being submitted, not just *which tools* are in use, and the only one that sees the 17 of 41 shadow agents in the example at the top of this guide that never touched a provider API in their own name.


**2. OAuth grant inventory.** Pull every OAuth-authorized application across Google Workspace (` users.tokens.list` ), Microsoft Entra ID, Slack and GitHub, and cross-reference against a maintained catalog of AI products. This catches the long tail (Otter, Fathom, Gong, Glean, Notion AI) that users authorized once and forgot.


**3. SaaS audit log filtering.** Google Workspace login and token audit logs, Microsoft 365 sign-in logs, Okta and Entra ID system logs, Slack admin logs and Salesforce Event Monitoring all reference AI tools used as authentication targets or connected apps. Filtered against an AI catalog, they surface every AI tool a user has signed into and every connected app acting through an API.


**4. Egress / SWG logs.** If the organization already runs Cloudflare Gateway, Zscaler or Netskope, its logs are useful. Most mid-market companies do not have one, which is why this method is fourth.


**5. Expense and procurement signals.** Ramp, Brex, Concur and corporate-card data show subscriptions that never went through procurement. Less timely, but useful for paid shadow AI that lives outside the SSO and SaaS log layer.


What each method catches, and what it misses:


Method


Catches


Misses


Network / DNS / egress logs

Read the **Misses** column carefully, because it explains why shadow AI inventories are always out of date: **every discovery method except the browser is blind to the free personal account, which is exactly where the problem is.** Detection tells you what happened. Only the browser and endpoint layer can intervene before it does, and only that layer sees an agent that borrows a human's session instead of asking for its own credential.


A complete shadow AI view fuses all five into a single inventory with a decision per tool:


An approve, observe or block decision per tool. Observe is the default for new tools, so discovery never silently turns into a block the business did not agree to.


## ✨ Beyond chatbots: MCP servers and the next wave of Shadow AI


The 2026 expansion of shadow AI is not another chatbot. It is agentic AI, language models that take actions on behalf of users via tool calls, and the most common transport for tool calls is the **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** .


Engineers stand up local MCP servers on their laptops to connect Claude, Cursor or other LLM clients to their local filesystem, Postgres, Slack, GitHub, AWS, Google Drive and browser sessions. Most run with no authentication, on` localhost` SSE transports, accessible to any process on the machine. A developer laptop with five running MCP servers is an undocumented broker that can read` ~/.ssh/id_rsa` ,` .env` files, browser cookie stores and corporate Slack DMs, and stream that context into a remote LLM on every prompt.


This is invisible to traditional Shadow IT discovery. The agent is local, the LLM is in the cloud, and no SaaS audit log records the tool invocations. Detection requires endpoint-level visibility into running MCP processes, their transport configuration, the tools they expose and the data they have accessed. The discovery method is covered in depth in[shadow MCP](https://www.strac.io/blog/shadow-mcp) .


A real MCP server inventory looks like this: a mix of stdio and SSE transports, several inactive servers that are still installed, and a handful of high-risk servers exposing filesystem or database access:


Inactive is not safe. A stopped MCP server with shell access is one config edit away from running again, which is why the inventory keeps it.


Two MCP-specific risks deserve to be called out:


- **Network-exposed servers.** An MCP server bound to` 0.0.0.0:3001` is reachable from any network the laptop joins. Anyone on that network can invoke its tools.
- **Over-broad filesystem access.** The default filesystem MCP server reaches the entire home directory unless explicitly scoped. Every "find me the relevant config" prompt is a free pass to read SSH keys and environment files.


Treating MCP as a shadow AI discovery problem (inventory, risk score, alert, remediate) is the right framing. MCP is also the clearest example of the bigger shift, which is the next section.


## ✨ Shadow AI agents: the 2026 version of the problem


A shadow AI agent is an AI agent or AI-enabled automation running inside your environment with real credentials that nobody registered, risk-assessed or owns. It is shadow AI with standing access and the ability to act. In the inventories we build, it takes five shapes:


- **OAuth grants to AI clients.** A user approved Claude, a custom GPT or a notetaker with` drive.readonly` or` gmail.readonly` . The AI client now acts on that user's behalf, continuously, against every file the user can open.
- **Local MCP servers.** Covered above. In the example environment at the top of this guide there are 26 of them across 19 workstations.
- **Computer-use agents driving a human's browser.** Cowork or a similar agent takes control of a Chrome tab where Alice is already logged into Salesforce and exports a report. No OAuth grant is created. No service account exists. Salesforce's audit log says Alice did it.
- **Automations on shared logins.** A Zapier or n8n flow signs into the CRM with team credentials. The provider sees the shared account, and the credential outlives everyone who knew it existed.
- **Bots with no owner.** An Agentforce case-triage bot or a Slack app set up by someone who has since changed teams. It still has its permissions. It still runs. Nobody would notice if it started doing something different.


Here is why this breaks the shadow AI programs most companies built. OAuth scanning and audit-log filtering are API-only methods. They see the grants and some of the bots, because those leave a record in a provider's admin API. They cannot see a local MCP server, an agent inside a human's browser session, or an automation on a shared login, because from the provider's point of view those are a human. In the example environment shown at the top of this guide, **17 of the 41 unsanctioned agents were found only by the endpoint or browser sensor.** An API-only product would have reported 24 and called the inventory complete.


Why API-only discovery misses shadow agents. Salesforce records Alice. The endpoint and browser sensors show the agent that actually clicked Export, and the finding states its confidence so a reviewer can disagree.


Three things in the shadow AI agents view at the top of this guide matter more than the counts:


1. **Every agent states how it was found.** "OAuth grant" is provider-native evidence. "Browser session" and "endpoint process" are Strac-correlated evidence. The distinction is shown, because an agent attributed through a shared login is a lower-confidence claim than one attributed through a unique` client_id` , and a reviewer should be able to disagree with it.
2. **Reach is joined to data, not scopes.** "Can reach sensitive data" means the agent's identity resolves to specific classified resources: 193 sensitive Drive files, a repo with 17 active secrets, a Salesforce object with customer PII. Of the 41 unsanctioned agents, 11 have that reach, and those 11 are the High findings. The other 30 are hygiene.
3. **The decision is bounded and reversible.** Sanction assigns an owner and moves the agent into the managed inventory. Revoke uses the provider's admin API where one exists (Google token revocation by` client_id` , Slack app restrict or uninstall) and otherwise generates the exact change and a console link. Block applies at the data layer, in the browser or on the endpoint, so the agent keeps running but stops receiving sensitive data. None of it requires write access on day one.


The findings that come out of this view are the same ones that drive Strac's agent security program: an unsanctioned agent that can access sensitive data (High), an ownerless live agent or credential (High), a shared human credential used by an agent (Medium to High), and an agent that can read secrets and execute (Critical). Severity is computed from six visible factors (sensitivity, action capability, breadth, sanctioning, observed use, attribution confidence) so a CISO can defend it in an audit. For the full method, start with[how to discover AI agents](https://www.strac.io/blog/discover-ai-agents) .


## How to build a Shadow AI policy that actually holds


Block-everything policies fail. Within two weeks, employees route around them by tethering to a phone hotspot, using a personal laptop, or finding an AI feature embedded in an already-approved SaaS. The pattern that actually works:


**Tier the tools, not the people.**


- **Approved** : enterprise-grade AI with SSO, admin controls, no training on customer data, signed DPA or BAA: ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude for Enterprise, Microsoft Copilot for M365, Google Gemini for Workspace, an internal LLM gateway.
- **Conditional** : allowed only behind a redaction layer that strips PII, PHI and secrets before the prompt leaves the browser. For tools the organization does not want to fully sanction but cannot reasonably block (Perplexity, Midjourney, niche industry tools).
- **Prohibited** : free-tier consumer accounts of any AI that trains on user data.


**Always provide an approved alternative for every prohibited tool.** Otherwise users go underground, and you lose the visibility you fought to gain.


**Add agent rules, because tool tiers do not cover standing access.** Four rules that hold up in practice: every agent has a named owner; any agent that can reach regulated data must be sanctioned; no single principal holds secrets access and execute capability; write, delete or admin permissions unused for 30 days are overprivilege and get narrowed. Preview each rule against the inventory before you enforce it, so you know how many owner requests and revocations it will generate.


**Map controls to whichever frameworks you carry.** A complete policy ties every control back to SOC 2 (CC1.4, CC6.1, CC9.2), ISO 27001 (A.5.19, A.5.23, A.8.16), ISO 42001 (clauses 8.2 to 8.4), NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act (Articles 16, 26, 50), GDPR (Articles 28, 32, 35) and HIPAA. Be framework-agnostic in implementation and framework-specific in evidence: the single control "every AI tool and agent processing customer data is inventoried, owned, risk-assessed and tied to a DPA" produces evidence under all of them at once.


For a deeper template, see the[AI Acceptable Use Policy template](https://www.strac.io/blog/ai-acceptable-use-policy-template) .


## What good Shadow AI governance looks like in practice


A mature shadow AI program produces four things, continuously:


1. **A live inventory** of every AI tool, model, agent and MCP server in use, with first-seen and last-seen timestamps, and for every agent an owner, the identity it runs as and the sensitive data it can reach.
2. **Per-tool and per-agent risk scores** weighted by data volume, sensitivity, OAuth scopes, vendor terms (training-on-prompt, retention, geography), and for agents the six severity factors above.
3. **Per-user risk views** so security can see which employees are highest exposure, with intervention as education rather than punishment.
4. **Continuous evidence** mapped to whatever frameworks the company carries, so compliance does not need a fire drill at audit time.


Two numbers tell you whether the program is working: the percentage of agents with an accountable owner, and the median time from finding to remediation. The companies that get this right in 2026 will treat shadow AI as an always-on capability, the way they treat Shadow IT, vulnerability management and CSPM today. The broader program is covered in[shadow AI governance](https://www.strac.io/blog/shadow-ai-governance) .


## ✨ How Strac discovers, governs and stops Shadow AI


Strac's approach to shadow AI is built around a single observation: **discovery without prompt-level visibility is a dashboard, not a control.** Knowing 18 AI tools are in use does not stop the customer record pasted into ChatGPT five minutes later. And knowing 187 agents exist does not tell you which 17 can reach sensitive data.


So Strac is built as an AI agent security platform that answers four questions for every AI tool, agent and automation it finds, and joins the answers in one graph: Agent → Principal → Permissions → Resources → Sensitive data.


- **Identity.** What is acting, who owns it, and which principal or credential it uses: a delegated OAuth grant, a bot or app identity, an IAM role, an API key, a human's browser session, or a shared login. Each gets an attribution confidence, and the shared-login and browser-session cases are labeled as correlated rather than provider-native.
- **Permissions.** What that principal can do, directly and through delegation. Granted and used are measured separately over a 30-day window, so overprivilege is a fact rather than a guess.
- **Activity.** What the agent actually did, from provider audit logs, the Anthropic and OpenAI compliance APIs, Salesforce Event Monitoring, GitHub's agent-session audit fields, and Strac's own MCP, browser and endpoint sensors.
- **Data.** What sensitive data it can reach and what it touched, joined to the classified inventory Strac already maintains across SaaS, cloud and endpoints. This is the pillar identity and SSPM tools lack.


Shadow AI tools and sanctioned agents in the same inventory. The 41 unmanaged rows are the shadow AI agents; the Agentforce bot with no owner and the Zapier flow on a shared login are the rows API-only discovery either misses or cannot attribute.


The discovery layer under that graph is what Strac has run for years, and it is what makes the inventory honest:


- **Browser-level visibility** through the Strac browser extension: AI domain visits, prompt content, file uploads, clipboard pastes into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Perplexity and 100+ other tools, plus an agent taking control of a logged-in tab. This is the layer that network, proxy and API-only products cannot match.
- **Endpoint visibility** for local Claude Code, Codex and Cursor processes, MCP configuration files, shell and tool execution, and secrets in the execution environment. See[what an endpoint DLP agent does](https://www.strac.io/blog/what-is-dlp-endpoint-agent) .
- **OAuth grant scanning** across Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack, GitHub and Salesforce: every AI app any employee has authorized, with scopes and the sensitive resources behind them.
- **SaaS audit log enrichment** : login, token and admin activity filtered against a maintained AI catalog, so a new tool or connected app is flagged the moment it is used.


**Visibility, not surveillance.** On the endpoint, Strac shows each AI service the fleet reaches, the app or browser that made the connection, the device and the user, and flags when sensitive data comes near an AI tool. It does this without reading a single prompt, and with no keystroke logs and no screenshots anywhere in the product. When you are ready to act, the same agent blocks sensitive files and uploads to unsanctioned tools.


**Enforcement on every surface.** Discovery tells you shadow AI exists. These controls decide what it can take with it:


- **Browser DLP** works on the personal, unmanaged account, which is precisely where shadow AI lives. It is the browser layer of[AI DLP](https://www.strac.io/blog/ai-dlp) .
- **Endpoint DLP** catches the installed assistants, local agents and MCP servers a browser control never sees.

## 🌶️ Spicy FAQs on Shadow AI


### What is shadow AI?


Shadow AI is any AI tool, model, agent or AI feature used inside a company that the IT, security or compliance team has not approved or inventoried. It includes free ChatGPT accounts, AI Chrome extensions, AI features auto-enabled inside SaaS like Notion or Slack, AI apps authorized via OAuth, locally running MCP servers, and agents or automations running on borrowed credentials. If you cannot answer "who used what AI, with what data, when, and under whose authorization," it is shadow AI.


### What is the difference between shadow AI and shadow IT?


Shadow IT is unsanctioned SaaS, hardware and scripts, primarily a vendor and license management problem that you can unwind by revoking the account. Shadow AI is focused on AI tools and agents, with three risks shadow IT did not have: prompt-level data leakage that cannot be recalled, prompt injection, and the AI vendor acting as a third-party data processor whose retention and training behavior is opaque.


### What are shadow AI agents?


Shadow AI agents are AI agents and AI-enabled automations running with real credentials that nobody registered, risk-assessed or owns: an AI client with a standing OAuth grant to Drive, a local MCP server with shell access, a computer-use agent driving an employee's logged-in browser, a Zapier flow on a shared CRM login, or an Agentforce bot whose creator left the team. They differ from shadow AI tools in that they hold standing access and act without a human reviewing each step, so risk is measured by what the agent can reach and do rather than by what one person pasted.


### How do you detect shadow AI agents that never create an OAuth grant?


With evidence from where the agent actually runs. An agent that drives a human's browser session or signs in with a shared login looks like a human in every provider audit log, so API-only discovery cannot see it. Strac's browser and endpoint sensors observe the agent process, the controlled tab, the tool call and the file lineage, correlate that with the provider's record of what the human account did, and label the attribution as correlated with its confidence factors shown. In a typical inventory that is how 17 of 41 unsanctioned agents are found.


### Can CASB or EDR detect shadow AI?


Partly. A CASB sees traffic to known AI domains and sanctioned apps, and EDR sees AI apps and processes running on a device. Neither sees what data went into a prompt on a personal account, and neither sees an AI agent acting through an OAuth grant or a human's browser session. Shadow AI detection needs browser and endpoint DLP that understands content, joined with OAuth and audit-log evidence.


### What is the biggest risk of shadow AI?


Most security teams answer "data leakage." The more accurate answer is **standing access** : an OAuth grant or agent credential that persists after the one-time paste. A single click can give an AI vendor or agent full read access to corporate Drive, Gmail or Slack, and the grant persists indefinitely, including after the employee leaves. A complete shadow AI program inventories OAuth grants and agent permissions alongside prompt content.


### Should we just block AI tools?


Blocking reliably fails. The tools are useful, employees are measured on output, and the alternative is one tab away on a personal device you do not manage. Organizations that ban AI outright mostly succeed in making shadow AI invisible rather than absent, and they get shadow AI agents on top. The approach that holds is to let people use AI, remove the sensitive data from the prompt (redact, warn or block per data class), and give every agent an owner and a scoped credential. If you do need to block a specific tool, see[how to block ChatGPT at work](https://www.strac.io/blog/how-to-block-chatgpt) .
